title: RNDC files for bankruptcy as distributor seeks buyers for remaining business
summary:
The US drinks distributor has entered Chapter 11 after months of selling operations across the country, with the court-supervised process intended to facilitate further sales and an orderly wind-down of its remaining business.

The post RNDC files for bankruptcy as distributor seeks buyers for remaining business appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
The US drinks distributor has entered Chapter 11 after months of selling operations across the country, with the court-supervised process intended to facilitate further sales and an orderly wind-down of its remaining business. Republic National Distributing Company (RNDC) has entered voluntary Chapter 11 proceedings as it looks to sell its remaining operations after a prolonged period of restructuring. The company announced that it filed for bankruptcy protection on 26 July, describing the move as a means of exploring court-supervised sale transactions while carrying out an orderly wind down of the business. National Distributing Company, Inc. has not been included in the filing. Among RNDC's joint ventures, only its Alaska operation forms part of the Chapter 11 process, with joint ventures in New York, Illinois, Ohio, Michigan, Indiana and Kentucky continuing outside the proceedings.

Restructuring reaches final stage

RNDC said the filing follows several months of divesting operations across multiple states in an effort to preserve jobs and maintain service for suppliers and customers. According to a company statement, those transactions safeguarded more than 5,000 jobs before its financial position ultimately required a court-supervised restructuring. "The court-supervised process is intended to give us the time and flexibility to continue working with parties that have expressed an interest in acquiring our other markets and conduct an orderly wind down of our remaining operations," the company said. RNDC added that it had secured a financing commitment from certain lenders to support the business during the Chapter 11 process and intends to continue meeting its obligations under transition service agreements linked to previously completed asset sales.

Mounting pressure

The distributor attributed its collapse to structural changes across the US drinks market. "Over time, our industry has evolved, consumer preferences have shifted and the wholesale environment has grown increasingly challenging," the company said. RNDC thanked suppliers, customers and employees for their support, adding that the decision to seek bankruptcy protection "was not made lightly".

Months of uncertainty

As previously reported by the drinks business, RNDC had already begun dismantling significant parts of its business following its withdrawal from California in September 2025 after losing major supplier accounts including Brown-Forman and Tito's. In January, the company agreed terms to sell operations in Florida, Hawaii, Illinois, Maryland, South Carolina, Virginia and Washington, D.C. to Reyes Beverage Group, preserving thousands of jobs and signalling that RNDC's national footprint would be significantly reduced. The California exit followed a series of major supplier departures that exposed growing pressure on the traditional three-tier distribution model, with Silicon Valley Bank warning at the time that RNDC's difficulties reflected wider structural challenges facing US wholesalers. The company had also lost several high-profile supplier relationships over the past two years, including Brown-Forman, Pernod Ricard and Treasury Wine Estates, as major producers increasingly reconsidered their distribution strategies.

title: From innovation to gastronomy: why Hungary is having a moment
summary:
Wines of Hungary undertook a UK-wide tour this year to show the wine trade just how much the Central European nation can offer. db spoke to those in attendance to understand how Hungary could be the next big thing

The post From innovation to gastronomy: why Hungary is having a moment appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Wines of Hungary undertook a UK-wide tour this year to show the wine trade just how much the Central European nation can offer. db spoke to those in attendance to understand how Hungary could be the next big thing.
Some countries are widely understood to be winemaking all-rounders. Others have built their reputations on an emblematic grape variety, or a region with a global following. It is very rare, however, to find a nation with a reputation that has been determined by just one very specific, highly local style. For many years, that was Hungary. The delectable, luscious sweet wines of Tokaj have all the hallmarks of iconic fine winemaking: a long-standing system of classification, a unique terroir and a transcendent quality both in youth and with substantial age. Often, the entire national reputation rested on the single Tokaj style. Times have changed, however. Tokaj has lost none of its lustre – it is still a winemaking powerhouse – but producers and Wines of Hungary, the sector’s marketing agency, are reminding the world that the rest of Hungary demands attention too. The very same qualities that commend Tokaj, such as its wealth of local varieties or its volcanic terroir, also apply to many other regions and styles. In fact, Wines of Hungary has been in full campaigning mode in the UK. Having hosted hit events in London, Birmingham and Bristol last year, it headed north to Edinburgh, Manchester and Leeds this spring. The roadshow of events brought a clear message: Hungary’s wines, no matter the style, are a perfect fit for the UK.

A packed programme

Given the diversity on offer in Hungary’s winemaking scene, summarising it in a single format would prove too much of a challenge. Instead, each of the stops on the roadshow provided a hub of information, producers and experiences. Central to each day was a masterclass led by Patrick Schmitt MW. Based on his own experiences visiting Hungary, and presenting a selection of his favourite wines, it was a whistle-stop tour of the country’s production. Indeed, as he noted, one of the core structuring features of his sessions was the need to cram in as much winemaking brilliance as a 90-minute slot would allow. A couple of core threads did emerge, however. With volcanic terroir, you are dealing with one of the wine world’s current favourite buzzwords. Yet Hungary, as a land of extinct volcanoes, sees it have a quantifiable effect on the wines. Moreover, volcanic geology is not a rare quirk of a particular winemaking region: it is a feature that defines the entire country. Schmitt also praised the “famously brilliant” Hungarians, a people responsible for the ballpoint pen, synthesising vitamin C and even the Rubik’s cube. That innovation is reflected in the winemaking. From the precision required in making botrytised sweet wines to the demands of traditional method sparkling winemaking, to matching current styles for fresh whites, Hungary is a nation well suited to adaptation. That adaptation also suggests something of Hungary’s diversity. The country is divided into six winemaking regions and, between them, 22 winemaking districts. Although most are defined by hills and extinct volcanoes, they vary hugely, with different centres for red and white winemaking, and a range of mesoclimates. You find diversity too in the grape varieties present: it is a mix of local stars like Furmint, Hárslevelű and Irsai Olivér; Central European stalwarts such as Kékfrankos (also known as Blaufränkisch) and Kadarka; and Hungarian spins on international varieties such as Cabernet Franc. The diversity was on full show in the walk-around tasting. With up to 36 wineries presenting each day, attendees had access to the breadth of Hungarian wine. Though Tokaj, the most familiar region, would be a draw for many, that was the beginning of the conversation, not the end. All this sampling took place in an environment that encouraged such discussions. The casual format ensured that relationships could be built rather than it being a sterile, academic tasting exercise. Food on the day – think steak pastries and mango cake – ensured that the convivial atmosphere continued, and that visitors could see the wines’ pairing potential. For both exhibitors and attendees, it proved an invaluable chance to grow Hungary’s presence in the UK.

Ongoing conversations

For Hungarian producers, developing markets and connecting with new partners is essential to long-term growth. What made these events really stand out, however, was a sense of dialogue far beyond commercial transaction. With the multi-faceted approach – masterclasses, food pairing, walk-around tastings and influencer-friendly moments – producers could dive into the UK’s wine ecosystem. For many, it provided a fascinating insight into the UK’s growth potential, and the niches where Hungarian wines can succeed. “What stood out to me most was how genuinely curious and engaged people were throughout the tour. The UK market is particularly exciting because consumers are open to discovering something new,” says Csilla Sebestyen of producer Sebestyén Pince Szekszárd. “I believe the UK offers excellent opportunities for Hungarian wines, as there is growing interest in lesser-known wine regions and indigenous grape varieties.” In particular, there was real excitement for the commercial opportunity provided by the UK’s food and wine scene. Though London is often considered the epicentre of the country’s gastronomic scene, the North of England and Scotland have real diversity in the on-trade, opening the door to exciting pairings and diversifying the wine list. “The cultural and gastronomic diversity in the UK is always surprising,” says Tamás Fröhlich, export manager at Gere Attila Pincészete. “If you enjoy good food, it’s only natural that you’ll want to pair it with high-quality drinks. During this trip, I experienced a real openness in the UK, especially in this segment. Following the basic principles of supply and demand, the only missing piece is the link that connects the two.” Thanks to the range of events and attendees, different producers could meet their needs in different ways. For Sebestyen, a particular highlight was the tasting in Edinburgh, where existing knowledge of Hungarian wines in Scotland’s capital meant that the audience was already invested. For Fröhlich, on the other hand, an influencer event stood out, where the wines could be presented “without preconceived ideas, just pure curiosity, genuine interest”. For all the attendees, however, it proved an opportunity to deepen ties with the UK. Although highly successful taken in isolation, the clearest benefits are as part of an ongoing programme of connection. “We are committed to investing in the development of our presence in the UK by visiting regularly and actively promoting our wines,” explains Sebestyen. “We also invite sommeliers and wine professionals to Hungary each year to discover our wines first-hand and learn more about our wine regions, traditions and winemaking philosophy. Our goal is to help more people experience the authenticity and diversity of Hungarian wine culture.” This sense of connection resonated for Fröhlich as well. “We hope this open and dynamic market will continue to deepen its interest in the diverse wines of Central Europe,” he comments. “The beauty of the Old World lies in its rich heritage, remarkable diversity and endless capacity to surprise. Our task is to remain present, foster meaningful relationships and continue connecting these exceptional wines with the right people.”

Made for the trade

Of course, what also matters with such events is bringing the wine to the end consumers. Although a day of discovery is a fantastic experience for the trade, the roadshow of events most proved its value by introducing buyers to wines and creating long-term ambassadors for Hungarian wine. That is essential in the UK market. Without local production dominating the shelves, the UK offers a global selection of wines. Thus, while the most famous wine nations will always fill shelves, there is plenty of space for other regions to find their niche. In settings such as restaurants and independent retailers, where consumers are often wine-literate, Hungary can even trade on its niche reputation. For many who attended Wines of Hungary’s UK events, they were discovering new things about the country. Even among the wine cognoscenti, there was evidence of room for Hungary’s profile to grow. “I discovered that Hungary produces a wide range of wines that are stylistically on-trend,” says Abi McCreath, product marketing manager at distributor Boutinot – “light, ‘Pinot-style’ reds, beautifully fresh and aromatic whites, exciting sparkling wine – or ‘buborek’, as it’s known in Hungarian – that could rival most crémants being produced, plus the infamous (and rightly so, in my opinion) sweet wines”. It was a chance to explore not only styles, but also the many stories behind the wines. Matilda Tsappis, owner of Michelin-starred restaurant Killiecrankie House, comments: “I hadn’t realised the breadth of grape varieties and wine styles produced – vibrant, traditional method sparkling Furmint, a grape variety called Juhfark drunk by the Hungarian nobility of old on their wedding night to guarantee a male heir… Who knew?” Certainly, by educating the trade, there is a trickle-down effect that reaches the consumer, but it is not just increased recognition that will commend Hungarian wines. With lighter styles, off-the-beaten track appeal and a compelling price-to-quality ratio, the wines are hitting the marks that consumers value. At Killiecrankie House, for instance, a saline, dry Furmint is a common fixture on the by-the-glass list. With the menu drawing on both Japanese inspiration and Scottish produce, seafood usually features heavily, with Furmint acting as a perfect foil. The fact that Hungarian wines offer good value helps immensely. Customers can opt for an option they may not know without having to buy an entire bottle. “Gastronomic, good-value wines will always go down well with guests,” explains Tsappis, “and the current trend for volcanic wines won’t hurt either.” It is an advantage that struck McCreath too. “Consumers are drinking lighter and fresher styles of wine, and I’d say both the Hungarian dry red and white wines I tasted at the event, and those within the Boutinot portfolio, are exactly that,” she says. “Consumers are enjoying discovering new regions and new grape varieties, and that’s precisely what Hungarian wine offers. Not only are they delicious and the quality extremely high, but the price point is excellent for wines that often go under the radar.” Indeed, this year’s events offered a strong sense of the opportunities open to Hungarian wine. The quality that Hungary offers has been evident for centuries, but the UK market is only just waking up to the range of wines on offer. With this concerted effort to tell the nation’s stories to the UK trade, Wines of Hungary is ensuring that the message reaches the everyday drinker.

title: “The only way to build a wine is by making fewer bottles than the market needs”
summary:
Success on La Place’s Hors Bordeaux campaign is a way to build brands and boost access for wineries, but as Sebastián Zuccardi, owner/winemaker at Argentina’s Familia Zuccardi, says, you cannot afford to be complacent. Arabella Mileham reports.

The post “The only way to build a wine is by making fewer bottles than the market needs” appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Success on La Place’s Hors Bordeaux campaign is a way to build brands and boost access for wineries, but as Sebastián Zuccardi, owner/winemaker at Argentina’s Familia Zuccardi, says, you cannot afford to be complacent. Arabella Mileham reports. Zuccardi was in London to present the two wines that are available on La Place: Finca Canal Uco, a single-vineyard Malbec expression from Paraje Altamira in the Uco Valley; and El Camino de Las Flores 2025, a high altitude non-malolatic Chardonnay from Monasterio in Tupungato, which is aged entirely in concrete vessels. Its inaugural release last year came out to great acclaim - db’s Bordeaux correspondent Colin Hay declared himself “an instant fan”, calling it “vibrant, racy and brilliantly crystalline” and awarding it 96 points. These two wines are in small production (the El Camino de Las Flores 2025 numbers only 2,000 bottles) represented now by five negociants on La Place. “We are not looking for volume on La Place, it's not why we are there, we are trying to access areas where our distribution is not arriving,” Zuccardi says. Argentina, for example, is not very strong in Asia, but the negociants’ market capillarity gives brand access to regions across Asia that could not otherwise be penetrated (although it now has a representative based in Hong Kong working across Asia, two in the US, one in Brazil and one in London). And while many people have built a big business through La Place, over the last three years, there’s no doubt business has become more complicated, which he admits is worrying. Bordeaux’s “crazy” unsustainable price rises during and immediately after the pandemic not only resulted in the present market malaise but also fuelled negociants to take on a great number of wines from outside Bordeaux. “I think the negociants took too much, but now there will be a curve, and it will stabilize,” Zuccardi shrugs. “The only way to build a wine is by making less bottles than the market needs - if you make one bottle more than the market needs you start talking about price.” “And I want to grow slowly and I don't want to reduce the prices.” It also takes time to understand the system. “When we started, I thought, ‘I have to put the wines in their stocks and they will do everything’, but they do the distribution, but they don't do the brand building, so you need to do work doing tastings,” he explains. “La Place helps to open doors, but you need to work, you need to go to the market, you need to be doing presentations,” he adds. “My passion is the vineyard and the winery, but today that is not enough. We have to go out and bring the message.” It is, he argues a form of evangelisation. “Evangelise, evangelise, evangelise! It's important because we are far [away] and not many people know the unique conditions that we have in the area. So, bringing the message [to them] is also important.” This is particularly the case where consumers have a fixed idea of Malbec from Argentina as very concentrated, black in colour, with a lot of oak. “But this is [only] one version of Malbec today,” Zuccardi says. “In the Uco Valley, you can see that many producers are not working like this - and we need to change the image of that for people. But this is a work that takes time.” “For many years, people thought that Malbec was a grape that was good for young wines. My feeling is that when it's coming from very good places, and we try to avoid overripe, over extraction, and overdraw, the aging potential is very long.” For Zuccardi, Malbec “is the best vehicle to express our places”, likening it to Nabbiolo in Barolo or Pinot Noir in Burgundy. “I like to say that we make mountain wines. Everything that happened in our area is in relationship with the mountain,” he says. It is the the rivers flowing down from the Andes that created the unique alluvial soils (granite covering by calcaire) the multitude of stones encouraging deep roots. It is also the reason for the cool temperatures and high sun exposure, which results in the slow maturation of the grapes. “We cultivate in a quite unique condition that is a cold climate with a very pure sunlight. I like to say that our wine has to talk about the freshness of the altitude and the intensity of the light and the management of the light is very important.”

Additional Tasting notes by Colin Hay

Finca Canal Uco (Zuccardi) 2013 (Mendoza; 100% Malbec; 1100 metres on the southern slopes of the Uco valley on the start of the alluvial fan; aged in 500 litre used oak14.5% alcohol). Big, bold, bloody and rich, certainly in comparison with the rather more ethereal recent vintages. And incredibly youthful. Plump and ample in frame, if a little closed at first. But that allows the stone fruit and, above all, the spicier elements to come through aromatically. The rose petals notes that in time become the central focus appear in the glass only later with a little gentle aeration. The wonderfully expressive limestone tannins bring massive grip to the mid-palate, wrestling the fruit to the tight and tense finish. Fresh, vivid, bright and crisp – if in fact rather more so on the palate than aromatically. Youthful and almost a little strict on the finish, this has considerable aging potential still. 93.

Finca Canal Uco (Zuccardi) 2016 (Mendoza; 100% Malbec; 1100 metres on the southern slopes of the Uco valley on the start of the alluvial fan; 14.5% alcohol; only 30% oak aged; vinified in concrete). A cool and comparatively wet vintage that really sorts the wheat from the chaff. It is gorgeous here and immediately captivating aromatically. Unlike the 2013, there’s no aromatic trace of the oak and that allows it to reveal immediately a lovely redolent bulbly florality that is the signature of the entire flight of wines here. In the mouth this is gracious, full and quite ample in frame. And here we find the beginning of the familiar crystallinity that is the Zuccardi calling card in the more recent vintage. Incredibly fresh once again, distinctly sapid on the finish and deceptively youthful. 95.

Finca Canal Uco (Zuccardi) 2019 (Mendoza; 100% Malbec; 1100 metres on the southern slopes of the Uco valley on the start of the alluvial fan; 14% alcohol). A great vintage and a very complete and composed wine. This is tight and compact, with a less ample frame but massive intensity and mid-palate density and concentration. The Zuccardi style that I recognise and love from the 2021, 2022 and 2023 is already present here, albeit now with a little more bottle maturation. The earlier vintages do not have quite the same finesse. Indeed, there’s a very rare, radiant purity to this. Loganberry, a little red cherry, with perfectly bright and crunchy berry fruits. Floral and herbal in equal measure and with those lovely beady limestone tannins. Ethereal, juicy and succulent with great finesse despite the density. Lifted and aerial, this finishes very much at the top of the palate. Supremely harmonious and fresh on the silken finish. Truly wonderful. 97.

Finca Canal Uco (Zuccardi) 2020 (Mendoza; 100% Malbec; 14.5% alcohol). A warm vintage, small in quantity, high in extract and relatively early picked. This is elegant, refined, subtle and finessed. It’s a little more intimate perhaps than the 2019, but no less aerial and lifted aromatically, the verticality from those gracious limestone tannins a little more apparent here than in the more ample vintages either side. There’s perhaps a little more fruit intensity than with the 2021. Very long and pure on the finish. Lithe, pure and very vertical in its aromatic presentation, this feels every inch a wine from a high altitude limestone terroir, as indeed it is. I love both the florality and the visceral intensity of the crushed raspberry and loganberry fruit, which is what this wine is all about. Lifted aromatically and tight on the palate with lots of purity and precision. Very fine. A most eloquent expression of its terroir. 96.

Finca Canal Uco (Zuccardi) 2021 (Mendoza; 100% Malbec; 14.5% alcohol). An excellent harvest. Cooler, not unlike the 2022, but a little drier. Intensely expressive and intensely floral aromatically, this is very vertical and aerial too. The parfumier’s essences of lilac and wild rosemary waft from the glass with a little dark purple peony too. Gracious and glowing, elegant and very fluid this has a wide and ample mouthful of fresh fruit juice pushing at the cheeks. Saline, with liquorice notes building towards the pleasingly sustained and sapid finish. Staggeringly fresh and incredibly vivid, with a pure, rippling, pulsating fruit signature, elongated by the gentle massage of the limestone tannins. Brilliantly juicy and electric. 96.

Finca Canal Uco (Zuccardi) 2022 (Mendoza; 100% Malbec; 14.5% alcohol). Beeswax and candlewax that I noted a year ago and now again almost exactly a year on. This is a little more substantial than the 2021 and maybe a little less immediately tense, with greater density and mid-palate concentration. The fruit is darker in shade and more intense still – assorted plump berries with a little damson and damson stone. There’s maybe a hint of walnut too and an almost Bordeaux-esque cassis and cedar combination. This is beguilingly composed with a very shapely spherical core outlined by the ultra-soft and fine-grained tannins. A wine of plunge-pool purity that is almost Pichon Comtesse-like in texture, but with Argentinian zing, spice and florality. Truly excellent. 97.

title: This is what fine wine cost in Gleneagles Hotel 60 years ago
summary:
Having been given a wine list from Scotland's Gleneagles Hotel printed in the mid-1960s, Patrick Schmitt MW looks at the cost of drinking Champagne, Bordeaux, Burgundy and Provençal rosé back then, versus today.

The post This is what fine wine cost in Gleneagles Hotel 60 years ago appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Having been given a wine list from Scotland's Gleneagles Hotel printed in the mid-1960s, Patrick Schmitt MW looks at the cost of drinking Champagne, Bordeaux, Burgundy and Provençal rosé back then, versus today.

There's been much recent commentary on the high cost of drinking wine in hotels and restaurants, including on this website, with the suggestion being that sought-after bottles are becoming prohibitively expensive in the on-trade, and that demand for them is softening as a result.

Restaurants derive a significant share of their profits from drinks, and typically apply a percentage margin to bottles – which makes higher-priced wines disproportionately expensive by the time they reach a wine list.

But how much has this actually changed? I've been able to draw some comparisons using a wine list from Gleneagles Hotel published around 1965, loaned to me by our long-standing city editor, Ron Emler.

Back then, as now, the Gleneagles Hotel in Perthshire was known for far more than its golf course, serving as a luxury playground for international elites, with Hollywood stars and star sportspeople among its summer guests.

Its wine list reflected the tastes of the era's rich socialites, featuring famous Champagne houses, first-growth Châteaux from Bordeaux, grands crus from Burgundy, and a single Provençal rosé – priced higher than either a premier cru Meursault or a deuxième cru claret on the same list.

Unlike today, the largest category of white wine by far was German (see pictures, bottom), split between Rhine and Moselle sections plus a lone 'Franconia' entry – comfortably outnumbering white Bordeaux, which was itself slightly ahead of Burgundy. Reds were mainly Bordeaux and Burgundy, with surprisingly few vintages stated; rosé ran to five entries, including Mateus from Portugal; and, curiously for a Scottish hotel, there was considerably more Cognac on the list than Scotch.

Drawing a direct comparison with Gleneagles' wine offer today is complicated by the fact that many of the historic wines are no longer made, and because dining at the resort now spans several restaurants, including the two-Michelin-starred Andrew Fairlie. Under the same ownership is also The Gleneagles Townhouse in Edinburgh, whose list is published online and could equally be used for comparison. For this piece, I've matched examples from the 1960s list against Andrew Fairlie's current list, and – where possible – against a contemporary retail source.

For the historic figures, the 1960s list is priced in shillings and pence (20 shillings to the pound). To convert into today's money, I've used a ×25 multiplier throughout, based on Bank of England/ONS composite price index data, which puts cumulative UK inflation between 1965 and 2026 at just over 25 times.

Champagne: Krug and Pol Roger

Krug is a natural place to start, given how central it is to Andrew Fairlie's own offering — the house is effectively an 'ambassador' for the restaurant. The prestige cuvée on the historic list, a 1961 Private Cuvée Extra Sec, is no longer made; it's a precursor to today's Krug Grande Cuvée.

On the 1960s list, the Krug is 63 shillings a bottle (£3.15) – £78.75 in today's money. A contemporary retail source, Castle & Co (a British wine and spirit merchant with outlets across London, Surrey, Oxfordshire and Dorset), shows fine Champagne selling on the shelf for around 25-35 shillings in the same period – £31.25 to £43.75 today – implying a restaurant markup of somewhere between 80% and 150%, depending on where in that retail range you benchmark.

Today, Krug Grande Cuvée 172ème Édition is £325 at Andrew Fairlie against a £240 retail price – a markup of about 35%. Krug has become dramatically more expensive in absolute terms, but the restaurant's percentage markup on it has, if anything, come down.

Pol Roger tells a different story. Its 'Extra Cuvée Réserve' is 58 shillings (£2.90) on the historic list – £72.50 today – against a 1960s retail price of 33 shillings (£1.65), or £41.25 adjusted, a markup of around 76%. The nearest equivalent today is Pol Roger 'White Foil' Brut NV, though Andrew Fairlie lists it only by the magnum, at £295, against a retail price of around £120 for the same format – a markup of roughly 146%. The size mismatch (bottle vs magnum) means this isn't a perfect comparison, but the direction is clear: the markup on this brand has expanded substantially.

German Riesling

Off-dry German wines dominated Gleneagles' 1960s list, and British taste has shifted so completely since that a direct comparison is difficult – very little German wine, sweet or dry, features on the on-trade list today. Andrew Fairlie's one Riesling Spätlese is a 2010 'Kreuznacher Krötenpfuhl' from Dönnhoff in the Nahe, at £112 against a retail price of around £50 – a markup of about 124%.

The 1960s list carries a Rauenthaler Burggraben Spätlese from the Rheingau (1963) at 40 shillings (£2) – £50 today. A retail comparison from the same era, Johannisberger Erntebringer Riesling Spätlese at 27 shillings and sixpence (£1.38), converts to around £34-35 today, implying a 1960s markup of roughly 45%. The two wines are from different sub-regions and producers, so this illustrates a category trend rather than a like-for-like comparison, but the direction – markup roughly tripling – is striking.

Bordeaux: Latour and d'Yquem

Château Latour appears on both lists. Andrew Fairlie carries the 2003 at £2,500 (£850 in retail, Hedonism Wines); the 1960s list carries the same first-growth Pauillac at 62 shillings and sixpence (£3.13, or £78 today), though without a stated vintage. Castle & Co's retail list from the same period shows Latour 1952 at 32 shillings (£1.60) – £40 today – implying a 1960s restaurant markup of around 95%, compared to almost 195% today.

Château d'Yquem shows a similar pattern. Andrew Fairlie lists a half bottle of the 2003 at £560 (which retails for around £150, a mark-up of 273%); the 1960s list has an entry at 60 shillings (£3, or £75 today) without a stated vintage or size, which I've taken to be a standard 75cl bottle. Castle & Co's retail range for d'Yquem in the same period was 31–36 shillings (£1.55–£1.80), or £38.75–£45 today, implying a 1960s markup of roughly 67-94%.

Rosé's fall from prominence

One of the more surprising findings is how rosé's status has changed. On Andrew Fairlie's current list, rosé has no section of its own – it sits within 'regional France', where a Rosé Cru Classé from Rimauresq, Côtes de Provence 2023, is £75 a bottle (and around £20 in retail). On the 1960s list, the sole Provençal entry, Château Sainte Roseline, was 35 shillings (£1.75, or £43.75 today) – nearly matching Château Léoville Poyferré 1954 at 34 shillings on the same list, and pricier than a Meursault Charmes at 28 shillings (£1.40, or £35 today). In the 1960s, in other words, in a fine dining environment, rosé wasn't a lesser category at all.

Spirits

A final, striking difference is in spirits. Despite being a Scottish hotel, the 1960s list carries more Cognac than Scotch. Today, the whisky list runs to more than 400 bottles, with Cognac a minor presence by comparison.

Beyond that, it should be noted that the list is almost entirely French, aside from the aforementioned emphasis on German whites. There is one Italian red (Chianti), nothing from Spain – aside from Sherry – and not a single reference for wine outside Europe.

What this tells us

Set side by side, the numbers suggest the story isn't simply that fine wine has got more expensive in restaurants – it's that markup behaves differently depending on how easily a diner can price-check a bottle elsewhere. Krug, the most recognisable name on this list, has seen its restaurant markup fall by comparison with the 1960s, even as its absolute price has soared – perhaps because a trophy Champagne brand is now heavily benchmarked by consumers against supermarket and merchant pricing, which limits how much a restaurant can add on percentage terms, or, in this specific case, because of Gleneagles role as a promoter of Krug, with a wide range of bottles at relatively accessible prices. Pol Roger and the German Riesling, by contrast, both show markup expanding sharply over the same period – categories with less retail price transparency appear to give restaurants more room to move.

The more striking shift, though, may be categorical rather than financial. German wine has gone from the single largest section of Gleneagles' white wine list to almost no presence at all; Cognac outnumbering Scotch in a Scottish hotel has completely inverted, with whisky now dominant; and rosé, once priced above a premier cru Meursault, no longer merits a section of its own. Sixty years on, fine wine costs more, but, notably, the regions and styles driving restaurant wine lists, and the pricing logic applied to them, have changed significantly.

title: 79 Bangkok venues ordered to shut down in safety crackdown
summary:
Thai Police have instructed 79 entertainment venues across Bangkok to cease operations due to license and safety breaches, in the wake of a deadly pub blaze that left 35 dead. 

The post 79 Bangkok venues ordered to shut down in safety crackdown appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content: Thai Police have instructed 79 entertainment venues across Bangkok to cease operations due to license and safety breaches, in the wake of a deadly pub blaze that left 35 dead.  Officials in Thailand’s capital have ordered 79 entertainment venues to shutter, after surveying 865 premises across the city as part of a broader safety campaign. The inspections follow a deadly pub blaze in Bangkok on July 13 that killed 35 people and left dozens wounded. The fire at the Rong Beer Na Lat Phrao pub is believed to have started after an overloaded electrical system sparked a short circuit. The emergency exit near the toilets was also reportedly bolted shut when the fire began. Following the inspections, which took place from 19 to 26 July, the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration split reviewed establishments into three groups – those that passed inspection, those ordered to make improvements and those ordered to halt operations. While 168 venues passed inspection, 618 were ordered to make improvements, with 570 in that category found to have shortcomings despite holding valid licenses.  Then, there were the 79 venues ordered to cease operations completely. Of this group, 19 were ordered to suspend live music performances as they did not hold the required licence, with another 60 temporarily shut down due to a lack of operating licences.  The aim of the campaign was to increase public confidence, and strengthen safety standards, according to City Hall.,  The inspections, conducted from July 19 to 26, covered 72 per cent of the city’s target of 1,204 establishments, Deputy Bangkok Governor Pornphrom Vikitsreth reported.

title: Thailand to ban alcohol sales during Buddhist holidays
summary:
Thailand, which is Southeast Asia’s second-largest economy, is set to ban alcohol sales for two days this week to mark the Buddhist holidays of Asalha Bucha Day and Buddhist Lent Day, the Royal Thai Police have announced.

The post Thailand to ban alcohol sales during Buddhist holidays appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Thailand, which is Southeast Asia’s second-largest economy, is set to ban alcohol sales for two days this week to mark the Buddhist holidays of Asalha Bucha Day and Buddhist Lent Day, the Royal Thai Police have announced. The restrictions will begin at 00:01 local time on 29 July and remain in force until midnight on 30 July. Under the ban, liquor stores, shops, convenience stores and most restaurants must suspend alcohol sales unless they qualify for exemptions under Thai law. Businesses found in breach of the ban could face fines of up to 10,000 baht, and up to six months in prison. Asalha Bucha Day, observed on 29 July, falls on the full moon of the eighth lunar month and commemorates the Buddha's first sermon, as well as the founding of the Four Noble Truths and the Sangha (the monastic community). It is a public holiday for government offices, banks and many private-sector businesses. Buddhist Lent Day, which follows on 30 July, commemorates the beginning of the three-month period of Buddhist Lent, when many monks remain in their temples to study and meditate throughout the rainy season. To mark the occasion, locals bring offerings like decorated candles, medicine, joss sticks and food to the temples for monks to use while they study. 

Exempt venues

The restrictions are set out in a 2025 notification issued by the Prime Minister's Office, which allows alcohol sales in five categories of exempt locations and events, including licensed entertainment venues, international airport terminals and select businesses in tourist areas that have been approved by the Public Health Minister. Hotels licensed under Thailand's hotel laws are also exempt, along with venues hosting major national or international events that have been specifically approved by the Public Health Minister following recommendations from the Tourism and Sports Minister. The Royal Thai Police said inspection teams will carry out country-wide checks during the two-day period, ensuring businesses are abiding by the legislation.

title: All the medallists from The Global Sangiovese Masters 2026
summary:
This year's Global Sangiovese Masters displayed the supreme quality of the grape – and the preeminence of one Italian region. Patricia Stefanowicz MW reports.

The post All the medallists from The Global Sangiovese Masters 2026 appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
This year's Global Sangiovese Masters displayed the supreme quality of the grape – and the preeminence of one Italian region. Patricia Stefanowicz MW reports. SANGIOVESE IS the quintessentially Italian variety and is grown practically everywhere in Italy. The grape is especially important in the central part of the country: Tuscany, Emilia-Romagna, the Marche and Umbria. Wine quality can vary but, as the judges found in this year’s Global Sangiovese Masters, given the right clones, careful vine-growing and judicious winemaking, the grape can provide superb wines, whether single-varietal or in blends. Traditionally, Chianti was a blend of varieties, with supporting roles played by Colorino, Canaiolo and Mammolo for Sangiovese. Nowadays, especially in Tuscany, ever since Bordeaux varieties were introduced to the coastal Bolgheri zone after the Second World War, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot are the most common partners. But experimentation continues apace, and nowadays Sangiovese blends with Syrah are being rewarded with much critical acclaim. When carefully made, these blends are exciting. That is not to take anything away from pure Sangiovese, and there were plenty of top-level wines (Gold and Master medal winners) among these expressions too. This year’s tasting gave the judges a good idea of what is being produced from Sangiovese, and the results were positive, with nine Gold medals, three Masters and one Grand Master awarded. The majority of the wines were from Tuscany, with a couple hailing from elsewhere in Italy, alongside examples from Australia and South Africa. As climate change continues, it will be interesting to see where the next wave of Sangioveses will come from.
At moderate price points, Australia performed well, with Silver medals for De Bortoli’s unoaked Rutherglen Estate Sangiovese and Langmeil’s Barossa Sangiovese-Barbera blend. And, during a very recent visit to Australia, this judge discovered that there are plenty more fantastic Sangiovese wines and blends to discover from the country where these two wines are produced. As is usually the case, Tuscany took top honours, with all 11 of our Golds and Masters coming from what is affectionately referred to by some British people as ‘Chianti-shire’. Not all the Italian winners were at silly prices either. Villa Saletta’s Luna and Basilica Cafaggio’s Chianti Classico are priced just under £20, and both earned well-deserved Golds. Querciabella’s ‘entry-level’ Chianti Classico priced in the mid-£20s, also achieved a Gold. Within the £30–£50 price bracket, the judges found excellent wines worthy of at least Silver medals, while Querciabella’s Chianti Classicos from two vintages (one of them priced just under £30) both earned Golds. The Chianti Classico Gran Selezione from RBW (Robin Baum Wines) and Conti di San Bonifacio’s Monteregio di Massa Marittima Riserva were awarded Masters. Above £50 there were Gold medal-winning wines from Villa Saletta for Riccardi IGT and Castello di Meleto for Vigna Casi Chianti Classico Gran Selezione DOCG.

SUBLIME POWERHOUSES

The finest wines we judged, at admittedly stratospheric prices, were from Querciabella. In addition to the Golds for the Chianti Classicos, the three wines from individual vineyard Gran Selezione sites in Greve, Radda and Lamole (SA-LA) were sublime powerhouses, with Greve taking home a Gold medal and SA-LA a Master. Radda achieved one of our highest ever judges’ marks and became the Grand Master of this tasting. These wines are admittedly youthful, but enjoyable even now – at least with very strong and savoury meat dishes. This Global Masters demonstrated that Sangiovese can be brilliant. The high number of Silver, Gold and Master medals dished out attest to that. And, despite escalating prices, the judges agreed that Sangiovese represents good value for money at various price points in 2026. A gastronomic joy, Sangiovese deserves a place in every wine enthusiast’s repertoire.

With high-quality judges and a unique sampling process, The Global Sangiovese Masters provides a chance for your wines to shine. The 2026 competition was judged on 27 May at House of Decant in London, employing experienced judges. The top entries were awarded Gold, Silver or Bronze medals according to their result, and those expressions that stood out as being outstanding received the ultimate accolades – the titles of Global Sangiovese Master or Grand Master. This report features medal winners only. title: Is Canadian fizz nearing its ‘Nirvana’ moment?
summary:
At a sparkling wine tasting in Ontario it was suggested that Canadian bubbles have reached "a critical moment", akin to when rock band Nirvana released its pivotal Nevermind album. Sarah Neish reports.

The post Is Canadian fizz nearing its ‘Nirvana’ moment? appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
At a sparkling wine tasting in Ontario it was suggested that Canadian bubbles have reached "a critical moment", akin to when rock band Nirvana released its pivotal Nevermind album. Sarah Neish reports. During the 16th annual International Cool Climate Chardonnay Celebration (i4C), which took place in Niagara from 16 to 19 July, Canadian wine writer Christopher Waters argued that the nation's sparkling wine offering is on the cusp of revolution. "Sparkling wine is about to crest," he said, comparing Canada's fizz scene in 2026 to the defining moment when Nirvana released its renowned album Nevermind in September 1991. The record turned the underground act into global superstars overnight, with breakout single Smells Like Teen Spirit dominating MTV and radio airwaves for months. According to Waters, "we've always had everything we need to make sparkling wine. We have the climate, we have the grapes in the ground. What we haven't had up to now is that knowledge transfer." The Canadian wine industry as a whole, he added "is predicated on adopting best practices from around the world and adopting them to make sense here." That is now happening, with Canadian producers "starting to take the reins and steer it [sparkling wine] in the cellar more, building texture and style."

New wave success

Much of this new wave of success can be attributed to Canada's escalating prowess with Chardonnay. While the variety "didn't used to be spoken about as loudly or as fully," Waters said, "Chardonnay is now something we can hang our hat on." The size of Canada and the country's rich spread of different climates and terroirs means that Canadian sparkling wine is also stylistically diverse, evidenced by a number of Blanc de Blancs included in the tasting, hailing from Prince Edward County, Niagara-on-the-Lake and Beamsville Bench in Ontario, to Kelowna in British Columbia. From distinctive matchstick and flint characteristics to sweeter lemon biscotti notes and rounded Brioche, the wines whispered of the unique corners they come from. Other producers have borrowed elements from renowned winemaking regions across the ocean and made them their own, such as Tantalus Vineyards in BC, which uses exclusively Champagne yeast in its sparkling wines after winemaker David Paterson paid a visit to the French region "to try and find the style we wanted."

Work in progress

Is Canada a great sparkling wine nation? "I think we are a work in progress. It's heading in that direction and we will get there," said Waters, who claimed that five or six years from now a sparkling wine tasting featuring expressions from all across Canada would prove electric. "And if you don't actually have dirt under your fingernails and are not making Canadian sparkling wine then your duty is to drink it, celebrate it, and support it," he added, because "this work will go away if people don't support it."

title: Louis Roederer enters Burgundy with Domaine Pierre Damoy acquisition
summary:
Champagne Louis Roederer has expanded into Burgundy for the first time after acquiring Domaine Pierre Damoy, adding some of the Côte de Nuits' most sought-after grand cru vineyards to its growing portfolio. The purchase comes as the Champagne house celebrates its 250th anniversary.

The post Louis Roederer enters Burgundy with Domaine Pierre Damoy acquisition appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Champagne Louis Roederer has expanded into Burgundy for the first time after acquiring Domaine Pierre Damoy, adding some of the Côte de Nuits' most sought-after grand cru vineyards to its growing portfolio. The purchase comes as the Champagne house celebrates its 250th anniversary. Champagne Louis Roederer has made its first move into Burgundy with the acquisition of Domaine Pierre Damoy, securing a collection of grand cru vineyards in Gevrey-Chambertin as the family-owned producer marks its 250th year. Completed on 24 July, the deal brings almost eight hectares of grand cru vineyards into the Roederer Collection, including parcels in Chambertin, Chambertin-Clos de Bèze and Chapelle-Chambertin. The acquisition also includes Clos Tamisot, a monopole vineyard in Gevrey-Chambertin. Financial terms of the transaction have not been disclosed.

A new chapter beyond Champagne

The estate will become part of the Roederer Collection, the group's portfolio of wineries spanning France, Portugal and the United States. Louis Roederer CEO Frédéric Rouzaud described the purchase as a milestone in the company's history. “In the year Louis Roederer celebrates its 250th anniversary, establishing a presence in Burgundy, one of the world's most prestigious wine regions, and becoming the steward of one of its great estates carries a special meaning for us,” he said. “Our mission now is to accompany this estate with humility and exacting standards, building on the remarkable work carried out by the Damoy family and preserving everything that makes it truly unique.” The acquisition represents a further step in Roederer's strategy of investing in premium wine estates beyond Champagne, adding one of Burgundy's most revered vineyard holdings to a collection that already encompasses producers across several leading wine regions.

Anniversary year continues

As previously reported by the drinks business, Louis Roederer has been marking its 250th anniversary with a series of high-profile announcements, including the launch of a late-release expression of Cristal 2008. Speaking at the unveiling in Reims, cellar master Jean-Baptiste Lécaillon described the wine as "the Cristal of Cristals", calling the 2008 vintage the benchmark expression of the maison's prestige cuvée. The late-release spent 13 years ageing on its lees before disgorgement and forms part of a broader programme to release Cristal at multiple stages of maturity. The Burgundy acquisition extends what has already been a landmark year for the Champagne house, broadening its presence beyond its home region at a time when it is reflecting on two and a half centuries of winemaking history.

Challenging backdrop for Champagne

The announcement also comes against a more cautious backdrop for the Champagne sector. Last week, Comité Champagne agreed to reduce the volume of grapes that may be sold from the 2026 harvest by 2% compared with last year, describing the move as part of an effort to rebalance stocks, preserve quality and maintain the long-term economic sustainability of the region.

title: Manchuela broadens wine styles and relaxes bottling rules
summary:
Spain's Manchuela DO has approved changes to its production rules that expand the range of wines permitted under the appellation and remove the requirement for wines to be bottled within the production area. The revisions also introduce a new authorised grape variety as the denomination continues to modernise its regulations.

The post Manchuela broadens wine styles and relaxes bottling rules appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Spain's Manchuela DO has approved changes to its production rules that expand the range of wines permitted under the appellation and remove the requirement for wines to be bottled within the production area. The revisions also introduce a new authorised grape variety as the denomination continues to modernise its regulations. Manchuela DO has approved a series of amendments to its appellation rules, allowing producers to make new categories of aged white and rosé wines, authorising an additional indigenous grape variety and removing the requirement for wines to be bottled within the denomination. The changes, published by the European Union as a "standard modification", do not alter the geographical area, product category or link between the wines and their place of origin. Instead, they update several aspects of the denomination's specification to give producers greater flexibility.

Aged whites and rosés recognised

The most significant change is the introduction of aged and matured white and rosé wines as recognised styles within the DO. Previously, the specification covered only the existing categories of still wines. Producers will now be able to market barrel-aged or otherwise matured white and rosé wines under the Manchuela appellation, provided they meet the revised production, analytical and quality requirements. The amendments also add Albillo Dorado to the list of authorised grape varieties, expanding the options available to growers seeking to diversify vineyard plantings.

Bottling restriction removed

Another notable revision is the removal of the obligation to bottle wines within the appellation's production area. According to the European Commission, the change is intended to provide producers with greater commercial flexibility without affecting the integrity or traceability of the protected designation of origin. A separate administrative amendment also removes the requirement for wineries to be registered with the appellation's interprofessional organisation, simplifying the wording of the production specification without altering how the denomination operates.

Building on a growing reputation

Located between the Júcar and Cabriel river valleys in eastern Castilla-La Mancha, Manchuela has spent much of the past two decades establishing itself as a quality-focused alternative to the region's historic bulk wine reputation. The denomination is particularly associated with old-vine Bobal, although producers also work with a broad range of indigenous and international varieties. As previously reported by the drinks business, Manchuela was identified by Spanish wine experts as one of the country's most overlooked wine regions. Speaking during Taste Spain earlier this year, María Naranjo, director of food and drink at Spanish trade organisation ICEX, described the denomination as "a very special region, that produces very different wines, offering something different to the world", pointing to its high-altitude vineyards and distinctive Bobal-based wines.
